title: Python Basics
description: Meet Python, store values in variables, explore data types and talk to the user.

subLevels.title: What is Python?
subLevels.summary: Your first look at Python and your very first line of code.

blocks.text: Python is a programming language — a way to give instructions to a computer using words that are close to plain English.

items: Free and works on every computer
Used by Google, Netflix, NASA and millions of developers

blocks.text: A program is just a list of instructions the computer follows from top to bottom.
The classic first program prints a message on the screen.

explanation: print is a built-in function that shows something on the screen.
The text inside the quotes is what gets shown.
The parentheses ( ) hold what you want to print.

blocks.text: You can call print as many times as you like. Each call starts on a new line.

explanation: Text needs quotes.
Numbers and maths don't — Python works out 2 + 3 for you.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Python reads your code line by line, starting at the top.
Lines starting with # are comments. Python ignores them — they are notes for humans.

blocks.code:
# This line is a comment
print("Comments are ignored")  # notes can go here too
explanation: Use comments to explain why your code does something.

questions.prompt: What does print() do in Python?
questions.explanation: print() shows whatever you put inside the parentheses on the screen. It does not restart or end the program, and only # makes a comment.
questions.hint: Think about what you saw appear after running print("Hello, World!").
optionFeedback: print() does not restart anything; Python runs each line once, from top to bottom.
Right: print() displays whatever is inside its parentheses on the screen.
Only the # symbol makes a comment; print() does the opposite and shows text to the user.
print() does not stop the program; the lines after it still run, one after another.

questions.explanation: Without quotes, 2 + 3 is maths, so Python works it out and prints 5. print shows the value without quotes, so it is not "5", and you would only see 2 + 3 if it were inside quotes.
questions.hint: Notice there are no quotes inside the parentheses, so Python treats it as maths.
optionFeedback: You would only see 2 + 3 if it were text inside quotes, like print("2 + 3").
print shows the value itself without quotes, so the quotes would not appear on screen.
Right: without quotes, 2 + 3 is maths, so Python works it out and prints the answer.
This is valid code: print can show the result of a sum, so nothing goes wrong.

questions.prompt: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
questions.explanation: In Python, everything after # on a line is a comment that Python ignores. //, -- and /* are used in other languages, not in Python.
questions.hint: Recall the Comments page: which symbol did those ignored lines begin with?
optionFeedback: // starts comments in some other languages, but Python does not use it for comments.
Right: Python ignores everything after # on a line.
-- is used for comments in some other languages, not in Python.
/* comes from other languages; Python does not treat it as the start of a comment.

questions.prompt: In what order does Python run your lines of code?
questions.explanation: Python reads your code line by line, starting at the top, so the first line runs first. It never picks lines at random or starts from the bottom.
questions.hint: Remember the key point about a program being a list of instructions.
optionFeedback: Python is predictable: it never picks lines at random, so the same code runs the same way each time.
Python starts with the first line you wrote, not the last one.
Right: Python reads your code line by line, starting with the first line.
Line length doesn't matter; Python follows the order the lines are written in.

subLevels.title: Variables
subLevels.summary: Give names to values so you can reuse them.

blocks.text: A variable is a named box that stores a value. You create one with the equals sign =

explanation: name stores the text "Asha".
age stores the number 21.
print(name) shows the value inside the box, not the word name.

blocks.text: Variables can change. The newest value replaces the old one.

explanation: The second line overwrites the first value.
Only the latest value is kept.

blocks.text: = means "store this value", not "is equal to".

items: Use letters, numbers and underscores: user_name, level2
Can't start with a number: 2name is not allowed
No spaces: use first_name, not first name
Names are case-sensitive: Age and age are different

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Pick names that describe the value, like total_price instead of x.

blocks.code:
apples = 4
oranges = 3
total = apples + oranges
print(total)
explanation: Python looks up the values of apples and oranges.
It adds them and stores the result in total.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly creates a variable?
questions.explanation: The variable name goes on the left, then a single =, then the value. Putting the value on the left is backwards, leaving out = stores nothing, and Python does not use the word var.
questions.hint: Recall which side of the = sign the variable name goes on.
optionFeedback: Right: the name goes on the left, then =, then the value to store.
This is backwards: the name must be on the left of = and the value on the right.
Without the = sign, Python is never told to store the value, so this is an error.
Python does not use the word var; you just write the name, =, and the value.

questions.hint: Think about what happens to the old value when you store a new one.
optionFeedback: 10 was the first value, but the second line replaces it before print runs.
Right: the newest value replaces the old one, so score holds 15.
Storing a new value replaces the old one; Python does not add them together.
score has no quotes in print(score), so Python shows the value stored in it, not the name.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: Names can use letters, digits and underscores but can't start with a digit or contain spaces/hyphens.
questions.hint: Go through the naming rules page and test each name against every rule.
optionFeedback: Variable names can't start with a number, so 2fast is not allowed.
Names can't contain spaces; Python would see two separate words.
Right: user_age uses only letters and an underscore, and starts with a letter.
A hyphen is not allowed in a name; only letters, numbers and underscores are.

questions.explanation: a is 3 and b is 4, so a + b is 7. print shows the values, not the words a + b, and numbers are added, so the answer is not 34.
questions.hint: Replace each variable with the number stored in it, then work out the sum.
optionFeedback: a and b have no quotes, so print shows the result of the sum, not the letters.
3 and 4 are numbers, so + does real maths with them; it does not write them side by side.
Right: a is 3 and b is 4, so a + b is 7.
Both variables are created before print uses them, so the code runs fine.

subLevels.title: Data Types
subLevels.summary: Text, whole numbers, decimals and True/False.

blocks.text: Python keeps track of what kind of value something is. The four you'll use most:
Use type() to ask Python what type a value is.

explanation: type() returns the kind of value.
Don't worry about the word class yet.

blocks.text: The same symbol can behave differently depending on the type.

explanation: With numbers, + adds.
With text, + joins strings together.

blocks.text: "5" (text) and 5 (number) are different things in Python.

explanation: int() turns the text "20" into the number 20.
Now maths works on it. str() and float() convert too.

questions.explanation: 3.14 has a decimal point, so it is a float. int is only for whole numbers like 42, and a str would need quotes.
questions.hint: Look closely at the dot in the number and recall the four main types.
optionFeedback: int is only for whole numbers like 42, but 3.14 has a decimal part.
A str is text and would need quotes, like "3.14".
Right: a number with a decimal point is a float.
bool only has two values, True and False, so 3.14 can't be a bool.

questions.explanation: Both values are strings, so + joins them into "23".
questions.hint: Notice the quotes around each value and recall how + treats text.
optionFeedback: You'd get 5 only with numbers; the quotes make these strings, so they are not added as maths.
Right: both values are strings, so + joins them side by side.
The + is outside the quotes, so Python performs it rather than printing it as text.
Joining two strings with + is allowed, so there is no error here.

questions.explanation: True without quotes is a bool. "True" and "yes" have quotes, so they are text (str), and 1.0 is a float.
questions.hint: A bool has no quotes and is one of exactly two special values.
optionFeedback: The quotes make this text (a str), even though the word inside looks like a bool.
Right: True without quotes is one of the two bool values.
1.0 has a decimal point, so it is a float, not a bool.
"yes" is in quotes, so it is a str; Python's bool values are only True and False.

questions.prompt: Which function converts "42" into a whole number?
questions.explanation: int() turns text like "42" into the whole number 42. float() gives a decimal number, str() makes text, and type() only tells you the type.
questions.hint: Remember that each conversion function is named after the type it produces.
optionFeedback: str() turns a value into text, which is the opposite of what we need here.
float() gives a decimal number such as 42.0, not a whole number.
type() only tells you what type a value is; it doesn't change it.
Right: int() turns text like "42" into the whole number 42.

subLevels.title: Input and Output
subLevels.summary: Ask the user a question and respond to them.

blocks.text: input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type something.

blocks.code:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello,", name)
blocks.output:
What is your name? Ravi
Hello, Ravi
explanation: The text inside input() is the question shown to the user.
Whatever they type is stored in name.
print can show several things separated by commas.

blocks.text: Even if the user types a number, input() gives you a string.
Convert input with int() or float() before doing maths.

blocks.code:
age = int(input("Age: "))
print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
blocks.output:
Age: 18
Next year you will be 19
explanation: input() reads the text "18".
int() turns it into the number 18.
Now age + 1 works.

blocks.text: f-strings let you place variables directly inside text. Put f before the quotes and wrap variables in { }.

blocks.code:
name = "Meera"
level = 1
print(f"{name} is on level {level}")

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: f-strings are the cleanest way to mix text and values.

questions.explanation: input() always returns what the user typed as a string.
questions.hint: Think about what type(age) printed even when the user typed 18.
optionFeedback: Even when the user types digits like 18, input() hands them back as text.
Right: input() always gives back what was typed as a string (text).
input() never turns the answer into True or False; it keeps the typed characters as text.
input() does give something back: the text the user typed, which you can store in a variable.

questions.prompt: How do you turn the user's answer into a whole number?
questions.explanation: input() gives the answer as text, and wrapping it in int() turns that text into a whole number. input(int()) puts int() inside the question instead, and Python has no number() function or .int.
questions.hint: Think about which job happens first: asking the question or converting the answer.
optionFeedback: Right: input() gets the text first, then int() turns it into a whole number.
This puts int() inside input(), so the conversion happens before the user has typed anything.
Python has no number() function; the converter for whole numbers is int().
There is no .int on text; conversion is done by wrapping the value in int( ).

questions.explanation: In an f-string, {x} is replaced with the value of x.
questions.hint: Remember what the f before the quotes does to anything inside curly braces.
optionFeedback: Because of the f before the quotes, {x} is replaced by the value, so the braces don't appear.
Inside an f-string, {x} means the value of x, not the letter x.
Right: {x} is replaced with the value of x, which is 5.
The f only marks the string as an f-string; it is not printed itself.

questions.prompt: What is shown to the user by input("Age: ")?
questions.explanation: The text inside input() is the question shown to the user before they type, so they see Age: . It is not an error, and Python shows your text, not the word input.
questions.hint: Think about the "What is your name?" example and when that text appeared.
optionFeedback: The text inside the parentheses is shown as a question before the user types.
Python runs input(); it shows your question text, not the name of the function.
Right: the text inside input() is displayed as the question.
Giving input() a question in quotes is correct, so there is no error.

projects.title: Party Bill Splitter
projects.summary: Ask for the bill and the number of friends, add a tip and split it fairly.

briefing.title: Build a Party Bill Splitter
text: You and your friends had dinner. This program asks for the bill and how many people there are, adds a 10% tip and tells everyone what to pay.
You build it one piece at a time. At each step you pick the right line of code and it appears in the program.
why: Splitting a bill is something you'll really do
It uses input(), type conversion, maths and f-strings: everything from Level 1
briefing.sampleOutput:
=== Bill Splitter ===
Your name: Asha
Total bill (Rs): 1200
How many people? 4
Thanks, Asha!
Tip (10%): Rs 120.0
Total with tip: Rs 1320.0
Each person pays: Rs 330.0

stages.title: Show a title
stages.instruction: Every program should tell the user what it does. Print a title line first.

question.explanation: Text goes inside quotes, and print is written in lowercase with brackets (1.1).

optionFeedback: Without quotes Python tries to read === as code. This is a SyntaxError.
Text goes inside quotes, and print is written in lowercase with brackets (1.1).
Python is case-sensitive: Print is not the same as print, so this is a NameError.
In Python 3, print needs brackets. This is a SyntaxError.

stages.title: Ask for a name
stages.instruction: Ask the user for their name and keep the answer in a variable called name.

question.prompt: Which line asks for the name and stores it?
question.explanation: input() shows the question and gives back what was typed; = stores it in name (1.2, 1.4).

optionFeedback: The variable name must be on the left of =. This is a SyntaxError.
This stores the words input(Your name: ) as text. Nothing is asked.
input() shows the question and gives back what was typed; = stores it in name (1.2, 1.4).
== compares, it doesn't store. name doesn't exist yet, so this is a NameError.

stages.title: Read the bill as a number
stages.instruction: The bill can have paise, like 1199.50, so it must become a decimal number before we do maths with it.

question.prompt: Which line reads the bill correctly?
question.explanation: input() always gives text. float() turns it into a decimal number (1.3).

optionFeedback: input() always gives text. float() turns it into a decimal number (1.3).
The bill would stay text, so bill * 0.1 would be a TypeError.
int() fails on decimals: typing 1199.50 would be a ValueError.
This tries to turn the question itself into a number, which is a ValueError.

stages.title: Count the people
stages.instruction: Now ask how many people are sharing. People come in whole numbers.

question.prompt: Which line reads the number of people?
question.explanation: int() wraps input() so the typed text becomes a whole number (1.4).

optionFeedback: The brackets are in the wrong order: int() runs on the question text first, a ValueError.
int() wraps input() so the typed text becomes a whole number (1.4).
int(input) tries to turn the input function itself into a number. This is a TypeError.
str() keeps it as text, so total / people would be a TypeError.

stages.title: Do the maths
stages.instruction: Work out a 10% tip, the total with the tip, and each person's share.

question.prompt: Which three lines do the maths?
options:
tip = bill * 0.1
total = bill + tip
share = total / people

tip = bill * 10%
total = bill + tip
share = total / people

tip = bill * 0.1
total = bill + tip
share = people / total

tip = bill * 0.1
total = bill * tip
share = total / people
question.explanation: 10% is 0.1 of the bill. Add it to the bill, then divide by the number of people (1.3).

optionFeedback: 10% is 0.1 of the bill. Add it to the bill, then divide by the number of people (1.3).
% means remainder in Python, not percent. bill * 10% is a SyntaxError.
Backwards: 4 / 1320 gives a tiny number, not each person's share.
The tip must be added, not multiplied: 1200 * 120 is far too much.

stages.title: Show the results
stages.instruction: Thank the user by name, then print the tip, the total and each share.

question.prompt: Which line thanks the user by name?
question.explanation: The f before the quotes lets {name} be replaced by the value (1.4).

optionFeedback: Without the f, Python prints the braces as they are: Thanks, {name}!
Without braces, the word name is printed instead of the value.
Text and a variable can't just sit next to each other. This is a SyntaxError.
The f before the quotes lets {name} be replaced by the value (1.4).

walkthrough: Line 2 prints a title so the user knows what the program does.
input() always gives text, so float() and int() turn the answers into numbers.
The tip is 0.1 of the bill (10%). The total adds the tip; the share divides it by the people.
f-strings put the values into the messages. Decimal results show .0, like 330.0.

cheatSheet.title: Python Basics

items.note: Show text. Text goes in quotes.
Commas print several values with spaces between.

items.code:
name = "Meera"
score = 10
score = score + 5
print(name, score)
items.note: = stores a value. A variable can be changed later.
Names: letters, digits and _, can't start with a digit, case matters.
Convert with int(), float() and str().
input() shows a question and always gives back text.

remember: Python is case-sensitive: print, not Print.
